clip.say: A workspace for evaluating clinical AI agents. You pick a real one — here, a scribe that drafts visit notes — and you just start talking. No setup, no dashboard to configure first.
Ask, in plain English, for a new judge — a focused reviewer that watches for one specific kind of mistake.

And it's done for real. The agent reads the case, authors a risk judge with genuine clinical nuance, and hands back an editable judge — with a full who, when, what, and why audit trail. Nothing hidden; every change recorded.
Then run the real thing — the actual council. Real model calls, not a cached replay.
The assistant can surface the cost gate, but it cannot spend. Only you authorize a paid run.

Here's the idea the whole system is built on. An AI judge can be confidently, fluently wrong. So a deterministic floor — grounded in the source the judge never read — checks every finding and quietly overrules any it can't ground in the actual record. That's a verdict a panel of judges, alone, can't give you.
Hold it against ground truth — the real source case, with the planted defect shown inline.
And it reads its own verdict honestly: which findings are true positives that match the planted defect, and which are over-fires to calibrate away.
So you calibrate the judge, and ask the only question that matters — did the change actually help?

The trainer compiles few-shot demos from a by-construction split and measures the honest, held-out delta on a fixed test set. And it tells the truth: if the tune didn't move the number, it shows you the loss — and refuses to loosen the gate to manufacture a win. No vanity metric. The real result, win or loss.

card.heading: Trust, by construction.
card.narration: Author. Run. Ground against the source. Calibrate honestly. The whole loop — live, every step audited. That's what makes a verdict you can actually trust. This is Lithrim.
